name: Silver Green
lede: Silver Green is a dusty sage from the Maerz and Paul dictionary, first recorded around 1884 and worn almost identically today by [[vetiver-green]], a color only 2.8 units away on screen.

sections.title: A sage with two names
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul file Silver Green at plate 21 F3, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS circular cites that same entry when it classes the color as grayish yellow green, about 4.6 units off its own block center [1]. The Munsell notation is 3.2GY 6.1/3.4 [1]. Our library also finds the identical hex used under the name Courge Green, so a reader who meets either name is looking at the same sage [1].

Silver Green's family word is "silver," the same root carried by [[silver-fern]] and [[silver-pink]], two other names from this same batch, though nothing in the record ties the three together beyond the shared word [1]. On screen, Vetiver Green sits only 2.8 units away, described here as almost the same; [[biscay-green]] and Celadon Green follow close behind at 3.1 and 3.3 [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this sage in 2.45 percent of 23,781 paintings, 582 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 300, as photographed [2]. That ranks it ahead of 77 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 48 of 1,674 paintings, present in 2.9 percent of the 1,674 paintings (48 of them) dated to that century, 2.2 times its museums' baseline rate [2].

Inside a painting it most often plays a light, 34 percent of its 300 appearances by lightness rank [2]. Alfred Sisley is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 6 of his 50 works, 5.6 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a painting dated to 916, 1,014 years before Maerz and Paul's circa-1884 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. On canvas it keeps company with Cedar Green and New Hay more than chance predicts, with lift of 10.9 and 6.6 [3].

origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color

openers: Silver Green and Vetiver Green sit only 2.8 color-units apart — two names for nearly the same dusty sage.
The same hex also answers to Courge Green in our library, a reminder that one color can carry two unrelated names.

issues: Only one book source (Maerz and Paul); no etymology for the name is documented.
The 916 first-seen painting is a look-alike match, not evidence the pigment existed then.
